p.src: Rotations of space are symmetries, and they act on many kinds of objects. They act on rigid bodies, on velocity vectors, on vector fields, and on quantum states. An ordinary vector is the simplest place to begin because its transformation can be pictured directly.

p.src: Rotations can also be combined. Rotate an object about one axis through one angle, and then rotate it about a second axis through a second angle. The final orientation is equivalent to a single rotation about some third axis through some third angle. Thus the product of two rotations is another rotation.

p.src: This product is an operation on transformations, not an addition of the two axis vectors. The first rotation changes the object on which the second acts. If $R_1$ is performed first and $R_2$ second, the combined operation is written $R_2R_1$. It is itself some $R_3$, even though finding the axis and angle of $R_3$ may be inconvenient. This closure under composition is the first reason to regard rotations as a group rather than merely as a list of geometrical motions.

A left-handed rotation through $\theta$ can equally be written as a right-handed rotation through $-\theta$, or as a right-handed rotation about $-\hat{\boldsymbol n}$.

p.src: Rotations are not commutative. A rotation about the $x$-axis followed by one about the $y$-axis generally gives a different orientation from the same two operations in the reverse order: $R_x(\alpha)R_y(\beta)\ne R_y(\beta)R_x(\alpha).$ The difference becomes second order when both angles are very small, which is why infinitesimal rotations can look almost commutative. The full group is nevertheless non-abelian.

p.src: The noncommutativity can be checked without any equations. Take a book or a box, mark one face as the front, and turn it by ninety degrees about the $x$-axis and then by ninety degrees about the $y$-axis. Return to the original orientation and reverse the order. The marked face ends in a different direction. For small angles the discrepancy is harder to see, but it has not vanished; it begins at the product of the two small angles.

p.src: A group by itself is abstract. To use it in physics we must say what objects it acts on. A emphrepresentation assigns an operator or matrix to each group element so that multiplication of group elements is reproduced by multiplication of the assigned matrices. Different physical objects can carry different representations of the same group. Vectors, spin-one states, and spin-one-half states will provide three examples.

p.src: Let an ordinary vector have components $\boldsymbol V=(V_x,V_y,V_z),\qquad V_i,\quad i=1,2,3.$ One may rotate the physical vector while holding the axes fixed, or rotate the coordinate axes while holding the vector fixed. The conventions differ, but in either description the components are mixed by a $3\times3$ matrix. For every axis-angle pair $(\hat{\boldsymbol n},\theta)$, write $V_i'=R_{ij}(\hat{\boldsymbol n},\theta)V_j,$ where a repeated index is summed.

p.src: The repeated index $j$ is a dummy label. Equation  means explicitly $V_i'=R_{i1}V_1+R_{i2}V_2+R_{i3}V_3$ for each output component $i$. The free index $i$ labels which component is being computed; the repeated $j$ is summed and may be renamed without changing the equation. Keeping those two roles separate prevents most index errors in the length-preservation argument.

p.src:
A true rotation preserves length. For the moment both $V_i$ and $R_{ij}$ are real, so $V_i'V_i'=V_iV_i$ for every vector. To expose the matrix condition, write the same transformation with different dummy indices: $V_i'=R_{ij}V_j,\qquad V_i'=R_{ik}V_k.$ Multiplying and summing over $i$ gives $\begin{aligned}
V_i'V_i'
 &=R_{ij}V_jR_{ik}V_k\\
 &=R_{ij}R_{ik}V_jV_k.\end{aligned}$ This equals $V_jV_j$ for every choice of $V$ only if $R_{ij}R_{ik}=\delta_{jk}.$ In matrix notation, $R^TR=\boldsymbol 1,$ and hence $R^{-1}=R^T.$ Transposition simply interchanges rows and columns.

p.src: Why must the coefficient be $\delta_{jk}$? The Kronecker delta sets $j=k$ under the sum: $\delta_{jk}V_jV_k=V_1^2+V_2^2+V_3^2.$ If $R_{ij}R_{ik}$ differed from $\delta_{jk}$, some direction or some cross term $V_jV_k$ would change the length. Since the equality is required for every possible vector, not merely for one chosen vector, the matrix coefficient itself must equal the identity.

Thus the matrix operations preserve the same closure, identity, inverse, and associative structure established geometrically.

p.src: The three-dimensional representation also acts on quantum states. A spin-one particle has three possible spin projections, $m=+1,\quad 0,\quad -1.$ Its spin state is therefore a three-component column of probability amplitudes. Rotating the particle, or changing the orientation of a magnetic field used to define the spin axis, mixes those three amplitudes by a three-dimensional representation of the rotation group.

For a spin-one particle, choose the basis $\lvert 1,+1\rangle,qquad
\lvert 1,0\rangle,qquad
\lvert 1,-1\rangle.$ A state is $\lvert\psi\rangle

u.src: Discrete and Continuous Symmetries
en: Discrete and Continuous Symmetries

p.src: Before turning to spin one-half, it helps to distinguish two broad kinds of groups. A reflection gives a simple discrete example. There is the identity and there is the reflection $P$; one either flips or does not flip. By contrast, a phase $e^{i\phi}$ depends continuously on $\phi$, and a spatial rotation depends continuously on its axis and angle. Such continuous groups are called Lie groups, after Sophus Lie; the name is pronounced Lee. Continuous symmetries will be the main concern, although discrete symmetries remain important.

p.src:
A spin-one-half system has two basis states. Relative to a chosen $z$-axis, $\lvert\uparrow\rangle=
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\lvert\downarrow\rangle=
\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}.$ A general state is a two-component spinor, $\lvert\psi\rangle=
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha_1\\\alpha_2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
|\alpha_1|^2+|\alpha_2|^2=1.$ The entries are complex. The choice $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=(1,0)$ is spin up, and $(0,1)$ is spin down. A general normalized combination describes a spin polarized along some other direction.

The determinant-one condition supplies tracelessness. For a small $2\times2$ matrix $A$, $\det(\boldsymbol 1+A)
=
\det
\begin{pmatrix}
1+A_{11}&A_{12}\\
A_{21}&1+A_{22}
\end{pmatrix}.$ Expanding, $\begin{aligned}
\det(\boldsymbol 1+A)
 &=(1+A_{11})(1+A_{22})-A_{12}A_{21}\\
 &=1+A_{11}+A_{22}+O(A^2)\\
 &=1+\operatorname{tr}A+O(A^2).\end{aligned}$ Applying this to $A=i\epsilon H$, $\det U=1+i\epsilon\,\operatorname{tr}H+O(\epsilon^2).$ Therefore $\det U=1$ requires $\operatorname{tr}H=0.$ The trace condition removes precisely the generator proportional to the identity matrix. A general Hermitian $2\times2$ matrix has four real parameters: two real diagonal entries and one complex off-diagonal entry. Its trace fixes one real combination, leaving three. This matches the three axes about which an infinitesimal spatial rotation can be made.

The infinitesimal generators of $SU(2)$ are thus traceless Hermitian $2\times2$ matrices. The three Pauli matrices form a basis: $\begin{aligned}
\sigma_x&=
\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
&
\sigma_y&=
\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},
\\[0.4em]
\sigma_z&=
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}$ Every generator can be written $H=a_x\sigma_x+a_y\sigma_y+a_z\sigma_z.$ A small rotation about the $x$-axis selects $\sigma_x$; one about the $y$-axis selects $\sigma_y$; and a rotation about any other axis selects the corresponding linear combination. In units with $\hbar=1$, the spin operators are $S_i=\frac{\sigma_i}{2}.$

p.src:
Combining representations can wait. We now leave spatial spin and return to quark color. A quark still has spin one-half, but its color is an independent three-state degree of freedom: $\lvert r\rangle,\qquad
\lvert g\rangle,\qquad
\lvert b\rangle.$ A general color state is $\begin{aligned}
\lvert q\rangle_{\mathrm{color}}
={}&
\alpha_r\lvert r\rangle
+\alpha_g\lvert g\rangle
+\alpha_b\lvert b\rangle,
\\
&|\alpha_r|^2+|\alpha_g|^2+|\alpha_b|^2=1.
\end{aligned}$ Equivalently, $q=
\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha_r\\
\alpha_g\\
\alpha_b
\end{pmatrix}.$ The squared magnitudes are the probabilities for red, green, and blue in a chosen color basis. The same triplet notation can assemble three quark field operators, $\psi=
\begin{pmatrix}
\psi_r\\
\psi_g\\
\psi_b
\end{pmatrix}.$

A simple interchange matrix may need an accompanying phase to make its determinant equal to one; the exchange is then embedded in the special-unitary group.

p.src: $SU(3)$ and the Eight Color Generators

u.src: $SU(3)$ and the Eight Color Generators
en: $SU(3)$ and the Eight Color Generators

p.src:
The continuous color transformation is $\begin{aligned}
q'&=Uq,
&
U^\dagger U&=\boldsymbol 1,
\\
\det U&=1,
&
U&\in SU(3).
\end{aligned}$ The mathematics is the same special-unitary construction used for spinors, but now $U$ is $3\times3$. This is not a rotation of physical space. It is a rotation in the internal color space.

p.src: The parameter count is immediate. A $3\times3$ complex matrix has nine complex entries, or eighteen real parameters. p.src: The nine real unitarity conditions may again be understood in terms of the columns of $U$. Three complex columns must each have unit norm, and every pair must be orthogonal. These conditions remove nine of the original eighteen real parameters. The determinant phase removes the tenth, leaving eight. This is the three-state analogue of the $8-4-1=3$ count for $SU(2)$.

p.src: The appearance of eight is the same fact that ultimately produces eight gluon species. Saying that there are not nine gluons because the determinant restriction removed one direction is only a mnemonic. More precisely, the nine color-anticolor matrices decompose into one color-singlet direction, proportional to the identity, and eight traceless directions. The eight traceless generators form the adjoint color structure carried by the QCD gluons.

What the parameter count has already shown is that there are eight independent directions in which an $SU(3)$ color transformation can begin to move away from the identity.

u.src: Color Symmetry Constrains QCD
en: Color Symmetry Constrains QCD

p.src: The basic symmetry statement is that the physics is invariant under the color transformation in Equation . This is the central internal symmetry of quantum chromodynamics. Mixing the color components is analogous in form to mixing spin-up and spin-down amplitudes, and those spinor transformations are in turn related to rotations of spatial directions, but the three spaces must not be confused.

p.src: Calling color a symmetry means that changing the color basis does not change physical predictions. Red, green, and blue are convenient names for three basis vectors, not three observable pigments. A simultaneous $SU(3)$ rotation of the color components must leave the form of the laws unchanged. This invariance is not an optional aesthetic feature; it is the organizing principle of QCD.

p.src: Symmetry restricts the Lagrangian. In the earlier $U(1)$ example, invariance under a common phase transformation constrained allowed terms to contain balanced factors of a field and its conjugate. In QCD, every term must likewise be invariant under the $SU(3)$ color transformation. That requirement has consequences for interactions, conserved quantities, and the form of the gluon field.

p.src: Suppose a proposed term carries an exposed color index. Under Equation  that index rotates, so the term cannot by itself be invariant. Allowed terms must contract color indices into invariant combinations or use gauge fields whose transformations compensate the change. This is the practical force of the symmetry principle: it rules out arbitrary couplings and organizes the interactions that remain.

That development belongs to the next stage. For now the essential structure is in place: a color triplet acted on by a special-unitary three-state symmetry with eight generators.

p.src: The calculation has gone as far into group theory as is needed for the moment. We began with rotations that can be drawn in ordinary space, passed to the matrices that act on vectors and spinors, and then reused the same logic in an internal color space. The next step can return to particle physics with the mathematical framework already available, rather than asking the formalism to carry the entire physical story at once.
